name: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
summary: From 376, Goths fleeing the Huns crossed the Danube and destroyed a Roman army at Adrianople, opening a century in which Germanic peoples and the Huns broke through the Rhine and Danube frontiers. Visigoths sacked Rome in 410, Vandals took Spain and then Roman Africa, and Attila's Huns ravaged Gaul and Italy before being checked in 451. Starved of land and taxes, the Western Empire became a shell run by barbarian generals until Odoacer deposed the last emperor in 476, leaving the West to successor kingdoms while the Eastern Empire survived.

sides.name: Goths, Vandals and other Germanic peoples

steps.label: 376 to 378
steps.title: Adrianople
steps.text: Driven west by the Huns, tens of thousands of Goths were allowed across the Danube in 376, but Roman officials starved and cheated them and they rose in revolt under Fritigern. Emperor Valens marched out of Constantinople without waiting for the western army of his nephew Gratian. At Adrianople in August 378 the Gothic cavalry fell on his legions, and Valens died with about two thirds of his army.

moves.label: Huns drive west across the steppe
Goths cross the Danube and revolt

events.name: Battle of Adrianople
events.text: The Gothic victory killed Emperor Valens and showed that a Roman field army could be destroyed in open battle.

steps.label: 406 to 410
steps.title: Rhine crossing and the sack of Rome
steps.text: On the last day of 406 Vandals, Alans and Suebi under Gunderic crossed the Rhine near Mainz, plundered Gaul and passed into Spain in 409. Meanwhile the Visigoths under Alaric, after years of fighting and bargaining with the general Stilicho, invaded Italy. Once Emperor Honorius had Stilicho executed in 408 nothing stopped Alaric, and in August 410 his men sacked Rome, the first fall of the city to a foreign enemy in eight centuries, while Britain was left to defend itself.

events.name: Crossing of the Rhine
events.text: Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed the Rhine near Mainz, and the western frontier was never fully restored.

events.name: Sack of Rome
events.text: Alaric's Visigoths plundered Rome for three days, a shock felt across the Roman world.

steps.label: 429 to 439
steps.title: Vandals take Africa
steps.text: In 429 the Vandal king Gaiseric ferried some 80,000 people across the Strait of Gibraltar into Roman Africa, the West's richest province and the source of Rome's grain. The Count of Africa, Boniface, was beaten and shut up in Hippo Regius, where the bishop Augustine died during the siege in 430. In 439 Gaiseric seized Carthage by surprise and made it the capital of a Vandal kingdom whose fleet could raid the whole western Mediterranean.

events.name: Siege of Hippo Regius
events.text: The Vandals besieged Hippo for over a year; Augustine of Hippo died inside the walls in August 430.

events.name: Fall of Carthage
events.text: Gaiseric took Carthage in peacetime, cutting Rome off from African grain and taxes.

steps.label: 451 to 452
steps.title: Attila and the Catalaunian Plains
steps.text: Attila, sole king of the Huns since 445, had already bled the Eastern Empire for tribute when he turned west in 451 with Huns, Ostrogoths and Gepids, sacking Metz and besieging Orleans. The Roman general Aetius gathered Romans, Visigoths under King Theodoric I, Franks and Alans, relieved Orleans and fought Attila to a standstill on the Catalaunian Plains, where Theodoric was killed. Attila invaded Italy the next year and razed Aquileia, but turned back after meeting Pope Leo I and died in 453, after which his empire fell apart.

events.name: Siege of Orleans
events.text: The city held out until the relief army of Aetius arrived.

events.name: Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
events.text: Aetius and the Visigoths checked Attila in one of the bloodiest battles of the age.

events.name: Sack of Aquileia
events.text: Attila destroyed Aquileia; refugees fled to the lagoons where Venice would later grow.

steps.label: 455 to 468
steps.title: The Vandal sack of Rome
steps.text: After Valentinian III murdered Aetius in 454 and was killed himself in 455, Gaiseric sailed from Carthage and plundered Rome for two weeks, carrying off the empress and her daughters. The Vandals seized Sardinia, Corsica, the Balearics and western Sicily and raided the Italian coasts every year. In 468 the two empires sent a huge joint armada under Basiliscus against Carthage, but Gaiseric burned it with fire ships off Cape Bon, ending the last real hope of saving the West.

events.name: Vandal sack of Rome
events.text: Gaiseric's Vandals plundered Rome for fourteen days.

events.name: Battle of Cape Bon
events.text: Vandal fire ships destroyed the joint Roman expedition against Carthage.

steps.label: 472 to 476
steps.title: The last emperor
steps.text: By the 470s the Western emperor ruled little more than Italy: Visigoths held most of Gaul and Spain, Burgundians the Rhone valley, Franks the north and Vandals Africa, and real power lay with barbarian generals. In 476 Odoacer, a Germanic officer, led the army in Italy in mutiny, killed the general Orestes and deposed his young son, the emperor Romulus Augustulus, at Ravenna. Odoacer sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople and ruled as king of Italy, while the Eastern Roman Empire would last almost another thousand years.

moves.label: Mutiny of the army in Italy

events.name: Deposition of Romulus Augustulus
events.text: Odoacer deposed the boy emperor, the conventional end of the Western Roman Empire.

name: Huna invasions of India
summary: The Alchon Huns, steppe invaders known in India as Hunas, crossed the Hindu Kush and attacked the Gupta Empire, which threw them back under Skandagupta about 460. Around 500 their kings Toramana and Mihirakula overran Gandhara, Punjab and central India as far as Malwa, until Indian rulers led by Yashodharman of Mandasor defeated Mihirakula about 528. The Huns were pushed back to Kashmir, but the wars shattered the Gupta Empire and India's classical age ended in a patchwork of regional kingdoms.

steps.label: c. 455 to 467
steps.title: Skandagupta holds the line
steps.text: Having taken Bactria and Kabul, the Alchon Huns under kings such as Khingila pushed through the passes into Gandhara and threatened the Gupta Empire, then at its height across northern India. Emperor Skandagupta led the Gupta army west and drove them back. His pillar inscription at Bhitari boasts that the earth shook when he met the Hunas in battle, and for a generation the Huns stayed beyond the Indus.

moves.label: Alchon Huns cross the Hindu Kush

events.name: Bhitari pillar inscription
events.text: Skandagupta's inscription at Bhitari records his victory over the Hunas.

steps.label: c. 484 to 510
steps.title: Toramana conquers the northwest
steps.text: After Skandagupta's death about 467 the Gupta Empire weakened through succession quarrels. Around 500 the Hun king Toramana led his horsemen out of Gandhara, overran Punjab and Rajasthan and reached Malwa in central India, where an inscription on a great stone boar at Eran is dated to his reign. In 510 the Gupta prince Bhanugupta fought a battle at Eran in which his general Goparaja was killed, and Gupta rule shrank toward the Ganges valley and Bengal.

fronts.label: Approximate limit of Hun rule, c. 510

events.name: Battle of Eran
events.text: A Gupta inscription at Eran records the battle in which Bhanugupta's general Goparaja fell; most historians link it to the Hun advance.

steps.label: c. 515 to 527
steps.title: Mihirakula's empire
steps.text: Toramana's son Mihirakula ruled from Sakala, modern Sialkot, over lands stretching from Gandhara and Kashmir to Gwalior, where an inscription is dated to his fifteenth regnal year. Buddhist sources remember him as a cruel persecutor who burned monasteries in Gandhara. The Chinese pilgrim Song Yun visited the Hun court in Gandhara about 520, when kindred Huns also ruled much of Central Asia.

fronts.label: Approximate limit of Hun rule, c. 520

events.name: Gwalior inscription of Mihirakula
events.text: An inscription at Gwalior fort dated in Mihirakula's reign shows Hun rule deep in central India.

steps.label: c. 528
steps.title: Yashodharman defeats Mihirakula
steps.text: Indian rulers finally combined against the Huns. Yashodharman, king of Mandasor in Malwa, defeated Mihirakula about 528 and set up victory pillars at Sondani claiming that the Hun king had bowed at his feet, while the pilgrim Xuanzang later credited the Gupta king Narasimhagupta Baladitya with capturing and releasing him. Mihirakula withdrew to Kashmir and Hun power in India was broken, but so was the Gupta Empire, which broke up into regional kingdoms within a few decades.

events.name: Battle of Sondani
events.text: Yashodharman's victory pillars at Sondani near Mandasor commemorate his defeat of Mihirakula.

name: Justinian's reconquests
summary: Emperor Justinian I set out to restore Roman rule in the West. His general Belisarius destroyed the Vandal kingdom in Africa in a single campaign in 533 to 534, but the war against the Ostrogoths in Italy dragged on for almost twenty years, through plague and a Gothic revival under Totila, until the eunuch general Narses won in 552 to 554. Africa, Italy and a strip of southern Spain returned to the empire, but Italy was left ruined and the empire overstretched, and the Lombards took much of Italy from 568.

steps.label: 533 to 534
steps.title: The Vandal War
steps.text: Using a Vandal succession dispute as a pretext, Justinian sent Belisarius with about 15,000 men in a fleet of 500 transports. They landed at Caput Vada in September 533 and marched up the coast, and when King Gelimer tried to trap them at Ad Decimum his divided army was routed and Carthage fell the next day. A second defeat at Tricamarum in December broke the Vandals, and Gelimer surrendered in March 534 and was paraded in triumph in Constantinople.

events.name: Battle of Ad Decimum
events.text: Belisarius routed Gelimer's divided army ten Roman miles from Carthage.

events.name: Battle of Tricamarum
events.text: The second defeat ended Vandal resistance; Gelimer fled and surrendered the next spring.

steps.label: 535 to 540
steps.title: Belisarius in Italy
steps.text: The murder of the pro-Roman Gothic queen Amalasuntha gave Justinian his reason to attack the Ostrogoths. In 535 Mundus took Dalmatia and Belisarius took Sicily almost without a fight, then crossed to Italy, stormed Naples and entered Rome in December 536. The new Gothic king Witiges besieged him there for a year from 537 but failed, and as Roman forces pushed north Belisarius closed in on Ravenna, which surrendered in 540 with Witiges inside.

fronts.label: Approximate front during the siege of Rome, 537

events.name: Siege of Rome
events.text: Belisarius held Rome against Witiges for a year until the Goths gave up.

events.name: Surrender of Ravenna
events.text: Witiges handed over the Gothic capital, apparently believing Belisarius would accept the western crown.

steps.label: 541 to 549
steps.title: Totila's revival
steps.text: Belisarius was recalled to face Persia, and in 541 the Goths chose the able Totila as king just as the Plague of Justinian began killing a large share of the empire's people. Totila routed the Roman commanders at Faenza in 542, took Naples in 543 and starved Rome into surrender in December 546. Belisarius came back with too few men and was recalled again in 549, leaving the Goths in control of most of Italy.

events.name: Battle of Faventia
events.text: Totila's small army routed a much larger Roman force near Faenza.

events.name: Totila takes Rome
events.text: Totila took the starving city after a long blockade.

steps.label: 551 to 554
steps.title: Narses ends the Gothic War
steps.text: Justinian finally gave the elderly eunuch Narses a large, well-paid army with Lombard and Herul allies, which marched around the head of the Adriatic to Ravenna in 552 and then down the Via Flaminia. At Taginae his archers and dismounted cavalry crushed the Goths and killed Totila, and the last Gothic king, Teias, fell at Mons Lactarius near Vesuvius that October. In 554 Narses destroyed a Frankish and Alamannic invasion on the Volturnus, and Italy was Roman again, but devastated.

events.name: Battle of Taginae
events.text: Narses' victory killed Totila and broke the Gothic army.

events.name: Battle of Mons Lactarius
events.text: Teias, the last Ostrogothic king, died in a two-day last stand.

events.name: Battle of the Volturnus
events.text: Narses annihilated a Frankish and Alamannic army near Casilinum.

name: Roman-Persian War of 602 to 628
summary: When the usurper Phocas murdered Emperor Maurice in 602, the Sasanian shah Khosrow II invaded to avenge his former patron and began the last and greatest war between Rome and Persia. Persian armies took Mesopotamia, Syria, Jerusalem and Egypt and in 626 besieged Constantinople together with the Avars, but Emperor Heraclius struck deep into Persia, won at Nineveh in 627 and forced a peace that restored the old frontier. The war exhausted both empires only a few years before the Arab conquests overwhelmed them.

steps.label: 602 to 610
steps.title: Khosrow avenges Maurice
steps.text: Khosrow II owed his throne to Emperor Maurice, so when the centurion Phocas killed Maurice and seized power in 602, the shah declared war. The Persians took the great frontier fortress of Dara in 604 and then overran Roman Mesopotamia and Armenia while Phocas purged his own generals. In 610 Heraclius, son of the governor of Africa, sailed from Carthage, overthrew Phocas and became emperor, but inherited a collapsing eastern front.

events.name: Siege of Dara
events.text: After a nine-month siege the Persians took Dara, the key Roman fortress in Mesopotamia.

events.name: Fall of Phocas
events.text: Heraclius's fleet reached Constantinople, Phocas was executed and Heraclius crowned.

steps.label: 611 to 619
steps.title: Persia conquers the East
steps.text: Heraclius's counterattack was beaten outside Antioch in 613, cutting the empire in two. Shahrbaraz took Damascus and in 614 Jerusalem, where thousands died and the True Cross was carried off to Ctesiphon, while Shahin's army reached Chalcedon across the Bosporus from Constantinople. From 618 Shahrbaraz invaded Egypt, and the fall of Alexandria in 619 cost the empire its richest province and the grain that fed the capital.

events.name: Battle of Antioch
events.text: Heraclius's defeat outside Antioch let the Persians split the empire.

events.name: Fall of Jerusalem
events.text: The Persians stormed Jerusalem after a three-week siege and took the True Cross.

events.name: Fall of Alexandria
events.text: Alexandria's fall gave Persia Egypt and its grain.

steps.label: 622 to 625
steps.title: Heraclius strikes back
steps.text: Heraclius bought a truce from the Avars, melted down church treasure to pay his troops and in 622 crossed to Asia Minor, where he trained a new army and beat Shahrbaraz. In 624 he marched through Armenia into Atropatene, the Persian heartland, and destroyed the great fire temple at Ganzak. Wintering in the Caucasus, he outmanoeuvred three Persian armies and in 625 defeated Shahrbaraz again at the bridge over the Sarus in Cilicia.

moves.label: Through the Caucasus to the Sarus, 625

events.name: Sack of Ganzak
events.text: Heraclius destroyed the fire temple of Adur Gushnasp, one of Zoroastrianism's holiest sites, in revenge for Jerusalem.

events.name: Battle of the Sarus
events.text: Heraclius beat Shahrbaraz at the bridge over the Sarus near modern Adana.

steps.title: Siege of Constantinople
steps.text: Khosrow staked everything on a combined strike at the capital: Shahrbaraz camped at Chalcedon on the Asian shore while the Avar khagan brought perhaps 80,000 Avars and Slavs to the land walls. Heraclius stayed in the east, sending part of his army back while his brother Theodore crushed Shahin's army, and went to Lazica to seal an alliance with the Western Turks. In August the defenders, led by the patrician Bonus and Patriarch Sergius, sank the Slav canoes trying to ferry Persians across the Bosporus, and the Avars withdrew.

moves.label: To Lazica to meet the Turks

events.name: Siege of Constantinople
events.text: The Theodosian Walls and the Roman fleet held, and the Avar khagan withdrew in August.

steps.label: 627 to 628
steps.title: Nineveh and peace
steps.text: With the Western Turks storming into the Caucasus and besieging Tiflis alongside him, Heraclius invaded Mesopotamia in autumn 627 and destroyed the army of Rhahzadh near the ruins of Nineveh in December. He sacked Khosrow's palace at Dastagird and approached Ctesiphon. Khosrow was overthrown and killed by his son Kavad II in February 628, and the new shah made peace, giving back all conquered lands and, in 630, the True Cross.

events.name: Battle of Nineveh
events.text: Heraclius killed Rhahzadh and destroyed the last Persian field army.

events.name: Peace of 628
events.text: Kavad II returned all Roman territory, ending the war on the old frontier.

name: Early Muslim conquests
summary: After the death of Muhammad, the Rashidun and then Umayyad caliphs led Arab armies out of Arabia against the exhausted Byzantine and Sasanian empires. Within a century the Caliphate stretched from Spain and Morocco to Central Asia and the Indus, though it failed to take Constantinople and was halted in Gaul and by the Berber Revolt. The conquests spread Islam and Arabic across a vast region and reshaped the medieval world.

steps.label: 632 to 636
steps.title: Yarmouk and Qadisiyyah
steps.text: After Muhammad's death in 632, Caliph Abu Bakr crushed the Ridda revolts and united Arabia, then sent armies against the Byzantine and Sasanian empires, both drained by their recent war. Khalid ibn al-Walid made a famous desert march from Iraq to Syria, Damascus fell in 634 to 635, and in 636 Arab armies won decisively at the Yarmouk against Heraclius's army and at al-Qadisiyyah against the Persian general Rostam.

events.name: Battle of the Yarmouk
events.text: A six-day battle that destroyed the Byzantine field army and cost the empire Syria.

events.name: Battle of al-Qadisiyyah
events.text: The Arab victory over Rostam opened Iraq to conquest.

steps.label: 639 to 642
steps.title: Egypt
steps.text: Amr ibn al-As led a small army from Palestine across Sinai into Egypt at the end of 639. After victory at Heliopolis in 640 and a long siege of the fortress of Babylon, the Byzantines agreed in November 641 to evacuate Alexandria. Egypt gave the Caliphate its grain, its shipyards and a base for the advance west.

events.name: Battle of Heliopolis
events.text: Amr defeated the Byzantine army of Egypt, opening the way to Babylon and Alexandria.

events.name: Treaty of Alexandria
events.text: The patriarch Cyrus agreed to hand over Alexandria, which the Arabs entered in 642.

steps.label: 637 to 651
steps.title: Fall of Persia
steps.text: The Arabs took the Sasanian capital Ctesiphon in 637 and founded garrison cities at Basra and Kufa. Under Caliph Umar they pushed onto the Iranian plateau, and the victory at Nahavand in 642, the Victory of Victories, ended organised Persian resistance. The last shah, Yazdegerd III, fled from province to province until he was killed near Merv in 651, and the Sasanian Empire was gone.

events.name: Fall of Ctesiphon
events.text: The Arabs took the Sasanian capital and its vast treasury.

events.name: Battle of Nahavand
events.text: The Victory of Victories destroyed the last great Sasanian army.

events.name: Death of Yazdegerd III
events.text: The last Sasanian shah was killed near Merv, ending the dynasty.

steps.label: 647 to 709
steps.title: North Africa
steps.text: Raids into Byzantine Africa began in 647, and in 670 Uqba ibn Nafi founded Kairouan as a permanent base. Uqba rode to the Atlantic in 681, but on his return the Berber chief Kusaila ambushed and killed him near Biskra, and Berber resistance under Kusaila and later the queen Kahina held up the conquest for twenty years. Hassan ibn al-Numan took Carthage, Byzantium's last stronghold, in 698, and by about 709 Musa ibn Nusayr had reached the Atlantic coast of Morocco.

moves.label: Kairouan and the ride to the Atlantic

events.name: Founding of Kairouan
events.text: Uqba ibn Nafi founded a garrison city that became the capital of Arab Africa.

events.name: Battle of Vescera
events.text: Kusaila's Berbers and Byzantine allies killed Uqba ibn Nafi near Biskra.

events.name: Fall of Carthage
events.text: Hassan ibn al-Numan took Byzantium's last major stronghold in Africa.

steps.label: 711 to 713
steps.title: Spain, Sindh and Transoxiana
steps.text: In 711 Tariq ibn Ziyad, a Berber commander serving Musa ibn Nusayr, crossed the strait that now bears his name, Gibraltar, and killed the Visigothic king Roderic at the Guadalete; within a few years the Visigothic kingdom had collapsed except in the northern mountains. In the same years Muhammad ibn Qasim conquered Sindh and Qutayba ibn Muslim took Bukhara and Samarkand, carrying the Caliphate to the Indus and the Jaxartes.

events.name: Battle of Guadalete
events.text: Tariq's army destroyed the Visigothic host and King Roderic was killed.

events.name: Fall of Debal
events.text: Muhammad ibn Qasim stormed the port of Debal at the mouth of the Indus and went on to conquer Sindh.

events.name: Capture of Samarkand
events.text: Qutayba ibn Muslim forced Samarkand to submit, completing the conquest of Transoxiana's heartland.

steps.label: 717 to 718
steps.title: Siege of Constantinople
steps.text: The Umayyads made their greatest effort against the Byzantine capital, sending a huge army under Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik and a large fleet. Emperor Leo III held the walls, Greek fire burned the Arab ships, and a harsh winter, Bulgar attacks and hunger forced a disastrous retreat in August 718. The failure kept the Caliphate out of southeastern Europe for centuries.

events.name: Siege of Constantinople
events.text: The failed siege saved Byzantium and blocked a Muslim advance into southeastern Europe.

steps.label: 720 to 732
steps.title: Tours
steps.text: From Spain the Umayyads took Narbonne and raided deep into Gaul, while in the Asturian mountains the Visigothic noble Pelagius won a small victory at Covadonga in 722. In 732 the governor of al-Andalus, Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi, crossed the Pyrenees, crushed Duke Odo of Aquitaine and sacked Bordeaux, then headed for the rich abbey of Tours. Charles Martel and the Franks stopped him between Poitiers and Tours, and he was killed in the battle.

events.name: Battle of the River Garonne
events.text: Abd al-Rahman routed Duke Odo of Aquitaine and sacked Bordeaux.

events.name: Battle of Tours
events.text: The Frankish infantry held firm and the Umayyad commander was killed, ending the raid.

steps.label: 739 to 750
steps.title: Limits of expansion
steps.text: The age of rapid conquest ended in a run of setbacks. In 740 Leo III destroyed an Umayyad army at Akroinon, and the same year the Berbers of the Maghreb, angered by heavy taxes and enslavement despite their conversion, rose in a great revolt that drove Arab rule out of Morocco and western Algeria. Overstretched and divided, the Umayyad dynasty was overthrown by the Abbasid revolution, whose armies from Khorasan won at the Zab in 750, and the Caliphate turned from expansion to consolidation.

events.name: Battle of Akroinon
events.text: Leo III destroyed a major Umayyad raiding army in western Anatolia.

events.name: Berber Revolt
events.text: A revolt beginning at Tangier destroyed Arab armies and ended Umayyad rule in the far Maghreb.

events.name: Battle of the Zab
events.text: The Abbasids defeated the last Umayyad caliph, Marwan II, and replaced his dynasty.

name: Battle of Talas and the An Lushan Rebellion
summary: In 751 an Abbasid army, helped by the defection of Karluk Turks, defeated the Tang general Gao Xianzhi near the Talas river, marking the western limit of Chinese power in Central Asia. Four years later the Tang frontier general An Lushan rebelled, took both Chinese capitals and proclaimed his own Yan dynasty. The Tang recovered only with the help of Uyghur cavalry and by 763 the rebellion was over, but China had suffered enormous loss of life, withdrawn its western garrisons and lost much central control to regional governors.

steps.title: Talas
steps.text: Tang China had extended its Anxi protectorate across the Tarim basin and over the Tian Shan, while the new Abbasid Caliphate was consolidating Transoxiana. When the Korean-born Tang general Gao Xianzhi overthrew the ruler of Tashkent, the city's allies appealed to the Arabs, and Gao marched west with Tang troops and Karluk and Ferghana auxiliaries. Near the Talas river in July 751 the Karluks changed sides in the middle of a five-day battle, and the Tang army was destroyed by the Abbasid general Ziyad ibn Salih.

events.name: Battle of Talas
events.text: The defection of the Karluks turned the battle, and Gao Xianzhi escaped with only a few thousand men.

steps.label: 755 to 756
steps.title: An Lushan takes the capitals
steps.text: An Lushan, a general of Sogdian and Turkic descent who commanded three frontier armies in the northeast, rebelled in December 755 against the chief minister Yang Guozhong. His veteran troops swept down the North China Plain, took Luoyang within weeks and in 756 broke through the Tong Pass, where Geshu Han's army was destroyed. Emperor Xuanzong fled toward Sichuan, his soldiers forced him to have his consort Yang Guifei killed at Mawei, and the crown prince proclaimed himself emperor Suzong at Lingwu.

events.name: Fall of Luoyang
events.text: An Lushan took the eastern capital and proclaimed himself emperor of Yan.

events.name: Battle of Tong Pass
events.text: Forced by the court to attack, Geshu Han's army was destroyed and the road to Chang'an lay open.

events.name: Mawei incident
events.text: Mutinous guards killed Yang Guozhong and forced the emperor to have Yang Guifei put to death.

steps.title: Recapture with Uyghur help
steps.text: An Lushan, half blind and violent, was murdered by his son An Qingxu in January 757. At Suiyang the Tang commander Zhang Xun held out for most of the year against a huge besieging army, shielding the rich Huai and Yangtze lands that fed the Tang war effort. In the autumn Guo Ziyi and the prince Li Chu, reinforced by Uyghur cavalry sent by the Uyghur khagan, won at Xiangji Temple, retook Chang'an and then Luoyang.

fronts.label: Rebel line on the Yellow River, late 757

events.name: Siege of Suiyang
events.text: Zhang Xun's garrison held for ten months before falling, but by then the south was safe.

events.name: Battle of Xiangji Temple
events.text: Tang and Uyghur troops won a hard battle south of Chang'an, and the capital was retaken days later.

events.name: Recapture of Luoyang
events.text: The rebels abandoned the eastern capital and fell back across the Yellow River.

steps.label: 758 to 763
steps.title: Shi Siming and the end of the rebellion
steps.text: A Tang siege of An Qingxu at Yecheng collapsed in 759 when a sandstorm scattered the besiegers and the rebel general Shi Siming arrived, killed An Qingxu, took over the rebellion and retook Luoyang. Shi Siming was in turn murdered by his son Shi Chaoyi in 761, and in 762 Tang and Uyghur forces recovered Luoyang for good. In early 763 Shi Chaoyi, deserted by his generals, killed himself, but the rebel commanders were pardoned as semi-independent governors and the Tang never regained their old strength.

events.name: Battle of Yecheng
events.text: Nine Tang armies without a supreme commander were scattered, giving the rebellion a second life.

events.name: Tang retake Luoyang
events.text: Tang and Uyghur troops recovered the eastern capital, which the Uyghurs then plundered.

events.name: End of the rebellion
events.text: Abandoned by his generals, Shi Chaoyi killed himself near Fanyang.

name: Charlemagne's wars
summary: Charlemagne, king of the Franks from 768, campaigned almost every year of his reign. He conquered the Lombard kingdom of Italy in 774, subdued and forcibly converted the pagan Saxons in thirty years of brutal fighting, carved out a Spanish March south of the Pyrenees and destroyed the Avar khaganate in the 790s. Crowned emperor in Rome in 800, he ruled the largest state in the West since Rome, the core of later France, Germany and Italy.

sides.name: Saxons, Lombards, Moors, Avars and Danes

steps.title: War on the Saxons
steps.text: The Saxons between the Rhine and the Elbe were pagan, independent and constantly raiding the Frankish border. In 772 Charlemagne marched from Worms, stormed the Saxon stronghold of Eresburg and cut down the Irminsul, their sacred pillar, opening a war that would last more than thirty years.

events.name: Destruction of the Irminsul
events.text: Charlemagne took Eresburg and destroyed the Saxons' holiest shrine.

steps.label: 773 to 774
steps.title: Conquest of the Lombards
steps.text: When the Lombard king Desiderius threatened Rome, Pope Adrian I called on Charlemagne. In 773 the Franks crossed the Alps in two columns, Charlemagne by the Mont Cenis and his uncle Bernard by the Great St Bernard, turned the Lombard defences at the Alpine passes and shut Desiderius up in Pavia. Pavia surrendered in June 774 after a nine-month siege, and Charlemagne made himself King of the Lombards.

events.name: Siege of Pavia
events.text: The Lombard capital surrendered and Desiderius ended his life in a Frankish monastery.

steps.title: Roncevaux and the Spanish March
steps.text: Invited by Muslim governors rebelling against the emir of Cordoba, Abd al-Rahman I, Charlemagne led two armies into Spain in 778, but Zaragoza shut its gates and news of a Saxon revolt called him home. As the army recrossed the Pyrenees, Basques ambushed the rearguard at Roncevaux Pass and killed its commanders, among them Roland, later the hero of the Song of Roland. The Franks returned more cautiously, taking Girona in 785.

events.name: Battle of Roncevaux Pass
events.text: Basque fighters destroyed the Frankish rearguard, killing Roland, prefect of the Breton March.

steps.label: 777 to 785
steps.title: Widukind and Verden
steps.text: Charlemagne held an assembly at Paderborn in the heart of Saxony in 777, but the Saxon noble Widukind repeatedly roused the country against Frankish rule and forced baptism. After the Saxons destroyed a Frankish army in the Suntel hills in 782, Charlemagne had some 4,500 Saxon prisoners beheaded at Verden. Campaigning even through the winters that followed, he wore down resistance until Widukind surrendered and was baptized in 785.

events.name: Battle of the Suntel
events.text: The Saxons wiped out a Frankish force in the Suntel hills.

events.name: Massacre of Verden
events.text: Charlemagne had some 4,500 Saxon captives executed.

events.name: Baptism of Widukind
events.text: The Saxon leader submitted and was baptized at Attigny with Charlemagne as godfather.

steps.label: 788 to 796
steps.title: Destruction of the Avars
steps.text: After deposing his cousin Duke Tassilo of Bavaria in 788, Charlemagne bordered the Avar khaganate, whose horsemen had raided Europe for two centuries. In 791 he led armies down both banks of the Danube as far as the Raab, and in 795 to 796 Duke Eric of Friuli and Charlemagne's son Pepin of Italy stormed the Ring, the Avars' great fortified camp, and carried off its treasure in fifteen wagons. Avar power collapsed and the middle Danube was opened to Frankish rule and missionaries.

moves.commander: Eric of Friuli and Pepin of Italy
moves.label: Assault on the Ring, 795 to 796

events.name: Fall of the Avar Ring
events.text: The Franks plundered the Avar treasure camp between the Danube and the Tisza; its exact site is unknown.

steps.label: 800 to 811
steps.title: Emperor of the West
steps.text: On Christmas Day 800 Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor of the Romans in St Peter's. His son Louis took Barcelona in 801 to anchor the Spanish March, and in 804 the last Saxons beyond the Elbe were deported and Saxony annexed. A new danger rose in the north, where King Godfred of Denmark fortified the Danevirke and raided Frisia; after Godfred's murder the Treaty of Heiligen in 811 fixed the border on the Eider river.

events.name: Coronation of Charlemagne
events.text: Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor, reviving the imperial title in the West.

events.name: Siege of Barcelona
events.text: Louis the Pious took Barcelona, which became the capital of the Spanish March.

events.name: Treaty of Heiligen
events.text: Franks and Danes agreed on the Eider as their border.

name: Viking invasions
summary: From the raid on Lindisfarne in 793, seafarers from Norway, Denmark and Sweden plundered, traded and settled from Ireland to the Volga. Danish armies conquered much of England until Alfred the Great and his heirs fought them back, a Viking chief received Normandy from the Frankish king in 911, Swedish Rus founded the state of Kyivan Rus, and in the early 1000s Danish kings ruled England itself. The Viking Age is conventionally ended in 1066, when Harald Hardrada died at Stamford Bridge and William of Normandy, a descendant of Vikings, conquered England.

steps.label: 793 to 800
steps.title: Lindisfarne
steps.text: In June 793 raiders from Norway sacked the monastery of Lindisfarne off the Northumbrian coast, killing monks and carrying off treasure and captives, and the scholar Alcuin wrote that such terror had never before been seen in Britain. Iona and other undefended island monasteries in Scotland and Ireland were struck within a few years. Fast, shallow-draught longships let small crews strike almost anywhere on the coasts and rivers of Europe and be gone before defenders could gather.

events.name: Raid on Lindisfarne
events.text: The sack of Lindisfarne is traditionally taken as the start of the Viking Age.

events.name: Raid on Iona
events.text: Raiders struck the monastery of St Columba, the first of several attacks.

steps.label: 834 to 845
steps.title: Raids become invasions
steps.text: From the 830s the raids grew into campaigns by fleets of a hundred ships or more, exploiting the civil wars among Charlemagne's grandsons. Norsemen founded Dublin in 841 as a fortified base, a fleet sacked Seville in 844 before being beaten at Tablada, and in 845 a Danish chieftain usually identified as Ragnar sailed up the Seine and took Paris, leaving only after Charles the Bald paid 7,000 pounds of silver.

events.name: Founding of Dublin
events.text: Norsemen built a fortified ship base that grew into Ireland's chief town.

events.name: Sack of Seville
events.text: Vikings sacked Seville but were routed at Tablada by the emir's army.

events.name: Siege of Paris
events.text: Ragnar's fleet took Paris and left only after a huge payment of silver.

steps.label: 865 to 886
steps.title: The Great Heathen Army
steps.text: In 865 a large Danish army led by Ivar the Boneless and Halfdan landed in East Anglia, bent on conquest rather than plunder. It took York in 866, killed King Edmund of East Anglia and overran Mercia, leaving Wessex under Alfred as the last English kingdom standing. Surprised by Guthrum at Chippenham in January 878, Alfred hid in the Somerset marshes, then raised the levies and crushed the Danes at Edington; Guthrum accepted baptism, and England was divided between Wessex and the Danish-ruled Danelaw.

events.name: Capture of York
events.text: The Danes seized York, which became the capital of a Viking kingdom.

events.name: Battle of Edington
events.text: Alfred's victory saved Wessex and forced Guthrum to make peace.

events.name: Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum
events.text: The treaty fixed the boundary between Wessex and the Danelaw.

steps.label: 860 to 907
steps.title: The Rus in the east
steps.text: Swedish Vikings, called Rus or Varangians, pushed down the rivers of eastern Europe to trade silver, furs and slaves with Byzantium and the Caliphate. A Rus fleet attacked Constantinople in 860, and according to the Russian Primary Chronicle Rurik took power in Novgorod about 862 and his kinsman Oleg seized Kyiv in 882, uniting the route from the Baltic to the Black Sea. Oleg's expedition against Constantinople in 907 won a favourable trade treaty, and his realm grew into Kyivan Rus.

events.name: Rus attack on Constantinople
events.text: A Rus fleet ravaged the suburbs of Constantinople before withdrawing.

events.name: Rurik at Novgorod
events.text: The chronicle says the Novgorodians invited Rurik to rule them.

events.name: Oleg takes Kyiv
events.text: Oleg killed Askold and Dir and made Kyiv his capital.

steps.label: 885 to 911
steps.title: Paris and Normandy
steps.text: In 885 a great Viking army of several hundred ships besieged Paris, which Count Odo held for nearly a year until Emperor Charles the Fat paid the Vikings off and let them ravage Burgundy. Viking bands then settled along the lower Seine under a leader named Rollo. After Rollo was beaten at Chartres in 911, King Charles the Simple granted him the lands around Rouen by the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte in return for baptism and defending the Seine, founding the duchy of Normandy.

events.name: Siege of Paris
events.text: Count Odo's defence held the city through 885 and 886, though the emperor then bought the Vikings off.

events.name: Battle of Chartres
events.text: Frankish forces drove Rollo back from Chartres.

events.name: Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte
events.text: Charles the Simple granted Rollo the lower Seine, the origin of Normandy.

steps.label: 910 to 954
steps.title: England fights back
steps.text: Alfred's son Edward the Elder and his daughter Aethelflaed, Lady of the Mercians, built fortified burhs and reconquered the southern Danelaw after victory at Tettenhall in 910. Alfred's grandson Aethelstan took York in 927 and in 937 crushed an alliance of Olaf Guthfrithson, Norse king of Dublin, with the Scots and Strathclyde Britons at Brunanburh. York changed hands several times more until its last Viking king, Eric Bloodaxe, was driven out and killed in 954, leaving England a single kingdom.

events.name: Battle of Tettenhall
events.text: The Northumbrian Danes were crushed on their way home from a raid.

events.name: Battle of Brunanburh
events.text: Aethelstan defeated the Norse and their Scottish allies; the site is disputed but often placed on the Wirral.

events.name: Death of Eric Bloodaxe
events.text: The last Viking king of York was killed at Stainmore.

steps.label: 980 to 1016
steps.title: The Danish conquest of England
steps.text: Raiding resumed in the 980s against the weak king Aethelred the Unready, who after the defeat at Maldon in 991 paid ever larger sums of Danegeld. In 1013 King Sweyn Forkbeard of Denmark conquered England, and after his death his son Cnut beat Edmund Ironside at Assandun in 1016 and became king of all England, later adding Norway to a North Sea empire. Far to the west, Norse settlers had meanwhile reached Iceland, Greenland and, about 1000, North America.

events.name: Battle of Maldon
events.text: Vikings killed Ealdorman Byrhtnoth, and England began paying Danegeld.

events.name: Battle of Assandun
events.text: Cnut's victory over Edmund Ironside made him king of England.

steps.title: Stamford Bridge and Hastings
steps.text: In September 1066 Harald Hardrada, king of Norway and the most famous Viking warrior of his day, landed in Yorkshire with Tostig, the exiled brother of King Harold Godwinson, and beat the northern earls at Fulford. Harold marched north at speed and destroyed the Norwegian army at Stamford Bridge, killing Hardrada. Three days later Duke William of Normandy, a descendant of Rollo, landed at Pevensey; Harold raced south and was killed at Hastings on 14 October, and the Norman Conquest is often taken as the end of the Viking Age.

events.name: Battle of Fulford
events.text: Hardrada and Tostig beat the earls Edwin and Morcar outside York.

events.name: Battle of Stamford Bridge
events.text: Harold Godwinson destroyed the Norwegian army and Harald Hardrada was killed.

events.name: Battle of Hastings
events.text: William of Normandy defeated and killed Harold, beginning the Norman conquest of England.
